53960.title: [Bug]: VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD deadlocks at kernel warmup on single GPU (TP=1) - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on GB10/sm_121
53960.body:
### Summary

Serving `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` with `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1` at `tensor_parallel_size=1` hangs permanently during startup. Engine init completes fully — weights load, KV cache is allocated, FlashInfer autotune finishes — and then the process goes silent before `init engine took Xs`. The API server never starts. No exception, no CUDA OOM, no kernel OOM-kill.

Reproduced 3/3 times, waiting 25, 60 and 60 minutes.

Full py-spy dump and container log (secrets redacted): https://gist.github.com/jdmays13/8b081bffc59d270d3125e6eac521f207

### Environment

- vLLM `v0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198`, image `vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next`
- NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark), `sm_121`, aarch64, driver 580.142, 128 GB unified memory
- Model: `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (135.2 GB on disk), `quantization=modelopt_fp4`
- `tensor_parallel_size=1`, `max_model_len=32768`, `speculative_config={"method":"mtp","num_spec_tokens":4}`
- `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1`

### Last log lines before the silence

```
[model_runner.py:407] Model loading took 80.28 GiB memory and 654.015720 seconds
[connector.py:231] PleOffload: registered 1 PleOffloadLayer(s) (dp_rank=0, tp_rank=0, ipc_addr=ipc:///tmp/ea99706f-...)
[kv_cache_utils.py:2258] GPU KV cache size: 271,610 tokens, Maximum concurrency for 32,768 tokens per request: 8.29x
[autotuner.py:852] flashinfer.jit: [Autotuner]: Autotuning process ends
[gpu_worker.py:919] Free memory on device (115.55/121.63 GiB) on startup
```

Then nothing for 46 minutes, until we killed it.

### py-spy: the deadlock

Main thread is blocked in the warmup forward pass:

```
Thread 365 (active): "MainThread"
    replay (torch/cuda/graphs.py:186)
    __call__ (vllm/compilation/cuda_graph.py:360)
    warmup_kernels (vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py:330)
        batch_req_state: (["_warmup_0_", "_warmup_1_", ...])
```

The PLE offload worker is blocked waiting for a request that never arrives:

```
Thread 532 (idle): "ple-offload-dp0"
    wait (threading.py:355)
        timeout: None
    get (queue.py:171)
        block: True
        timeout: None
    _request_loop (vllm/v1/ple_offload/connector.py:263)
        self: <PleOffloadConnector at 0x...>
        ipc_addr: "ipc:///tmp/1bcc22d1-..."
        socket: <Socket at 0x...>
        request: <PleOffloadRequest at 0x...>
```

The warmup forward needs n-gram/PLE rows to make progress. The worker that would supply them is parked in `Queue.get(block=True, timeout=None)`. Neither side advances, and because both waits are untimed there is no failure — just an indefinite hang that is indistinguishable from a slow load.

### `--enforce-eager` does not help

With `enforce_eager=True` (confirmed in the logged engine config) CUDA graph capture is skipped entirely, and startup still hangs at the same point with the same silence. So this is not specific to graph replay — removing graphs only changes where the main thread waits, not that it waits.

### The offload itself works

Worth stating, since it isolates the bug to readiness rather than to the feature: resident memory is **80.28 GiB** for a 135.2 GB checkpoint. The ~51.2 GB n-gram table (`ngram_vocab_size_base=20000000` × `ple_embed_dim=2560`) is genuinely kept out of device memory, which is exactly what the flag promises and is what makes this model viable on a 128 GB box at all. It simply never becomes ready to serve.

### Possibly relevant

The documented PLE-offload example uses `--tensor-parallel-size 4`, and the validated recipes are TP2/TP4 on GB300, so TP=1 may be an untested path. #51340 reports a superficially similar warmup hang from missing inter-rank synchronization, though that one is multi-node. #53908 requests auxiliary-GPU offloading for these same embeddings — related feature, different target.

Happy to run further diagnostics on this hardware if it would help; the box is available and reproducing takes about 15 minutes.

Same image (`vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next`, `sha256:fc120ece0a38`, vllm `0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198`), same checkpoint `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, TP=1, `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1`.

Byte-for-byte the same two frames you captured:

```
MainThread (active, 100% CPU):
    replay (torch/cuda/graphs.py:186)
    __call__ (vllm/compilation/cuda_graph.py:360)
    warmup_kernels (vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py:330)
    compile_or_warm_up_model (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:925)
    collective_rpc (vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:103)

"ple-offload-dp0" (idle):
    get (queue.py:171)          block=True, timeout=None
    _request_loop (vllm/v1/ple_offload/connector.py:263)
```

Details from my side that may narrow it, originally posted on #53896 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53896#issuecomment-5429590952):

**It is not sm_121, aarch64, unified memory, or MTP.** Our configs differ on all of those — I ran `max_model_len=65536`, no speculative decoding, discrete VRAM, x86 — and the hang is identical. The only things we share are **TP=1** and **`VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1`**. Note `uniproc_executor` in the stack above; the PR's own tests include `test_only_dp0_tp0_spawns_shared_ple_offload_worker`, so the TP=1 path is plumbed differently and looks unexercised.

**`VLLM_PLE_OFFLOAD_READY_TIMEOUT` does not bound it.** I lowered it to 120 s specifically to force a fast failure; the process was still spinning 6 minutes later with no exception. Neither wait is on the path that timeout guards, so there is no deadline anywhere — which is why it presents as an indefinite hang rather than an error. Agreed with your read that the untimed `Queue.get` is the core of it.

**Host RAM never rises**, so the ~48 GiB PLE table is never loaded — the offload worker parks before doing any work.

**There is a second, separate hang behind this one.** Setting `--enforce-eager` breaks the graph-replay deadlock (the stack leaves `torch/cuda/graphs.py` entirely), but startup then hangs in the dilated short-conv prefill instead:

```
MainThread (active):
    _short_conv_dilated_prefill_batched (vllm/models/qwen3_8_flash_next/nvidia/ple_layer.py:822)
    _short_conv_dilated_dispatch (.../ple_layer.py:1113)
    _short_conv (.../ple_layer.py:1189)
    qwen3_8_flash_next_ple_short_conv (.../ple_layer.py:1243)
    execute_model (vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:1726)
```

Identical across three py-spy samples 8 s apart — no progress. So `--enforce-eager` is not a workaround; it moves the hang rather than removing it. Worth knowing before anyone suggests it here.

Also for completeness: I applied @OsakaTX's hybrid-quant gate workaround from #53896 (force `Qwen3_8FlashNextPLEFp8EmbeddingMethod()` in `_get_ple_embedding_quant_method()`, since the RadixArk checkpoint is modelopt NVFP4 experts + FP8 PLE shards and so never reaches the `Fp8Config` branch). It does prevent the `ngram_embedding.weight_scale` `ValueError` at load time, but it changes neither hang above — both happen after weights are loaded. NB the module path in this image is `vllm/models/qwen3_8_flash_next/nvidia/ple_layer.py`, not `qwen4_exp/...`.

Reproduced 5/5 boots here. Happy to test a patch on sm_120 x86 if that is useful alongside your GB10.

@jhsmith409's instinct about `uniproc_executor` looks right, and there is a diagnosis and a
workaround for it — **credit to [dolf3131](https://github.com/dolf3131/qwen3.8-flash-next-dgx-spark),
who found this independently** and documented it; I am only relaying it here because two people
are blocked on something already solved.

`spawn_ple_offload()` and `wait_ple_offload_ready()` are called from
`vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py` and **nowhere else**. `uniproc_executor.py` has no such
call, and vLLM selects the uniproc executor by default at TP=1 — so with
`VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1` the offload worker is **never spawned**, and the GPU side then waits
forever on a peer that does not exist.

That fits every symptom in this thread: the untimed `Queue.get`, `VLLM_PLE_OFFLOAD_READY_TIMEOUT`
not bounding anything (neither wait is on the path it guards), host RAM never rising, and the
hang being identical on sm_121/aarch64/unified and sm_120/x86/discrete — an executor-selection
bug is hardware-independent by construction.

**Workaround:** `--distributed-executor-backend mp`, which forces the multiproc executor at one
GPU.

**Diagnostic, settles it in seconds:**

```bash
docker exec <container> ps -eo pid,rss,comm
# no PleOffloadWorker => it was never spawned
```

Their note adds that they also saw **no disk I/O at all** during the hang and that the announced
IPC socket never appeared in `/tmp` — both consistent with a worker that does not exist rather
than one that is slow.

**Scope of my own claim:** I have not yet reproduced this myself — same image
(`sha256:fc120ece0a38`, `0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198`) and a GB10, but my run is still pending. I am
posting now rather than after because the information unblocks people today. I will follow up
with a confirmation or a correction.

_Disclosure: AI-assisted analysis (Claude Code); the diagnosis relayed here is dolf3131's, not mine._

The `uniproc_executor` gap described above was fixed upstream this morning: PR #53899 picked up commit 95dc96d1d012 ("[BugFix] fix PLE-offload initialization in uniproc executor", 2026-08-27 06:00 UTC). The change is five lines in `vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py` -- `spawn_ple_offload()` after `init_device()` and `wait_ple_offload_ready()` after `load_model()`, both gated on `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD` -- i.e. exactly the two calls that previously existed only in `multiproc_executor`, plus a regression test (`test_uniproc_executor_starts_ple_worker_around_model_load`).

Until a build containing that commit, the `--distributed-executor-backend mp` workaround from the previous comment is the practical route (the `vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next` image referenced here, `g8e685d198`, predates the fix). A quick way to tell which side you are on: with offload enabled, `ps` should show the PLE offload worker process; if it is absent while the in-engine offload thread is parked in `Queue.get`, you are hitting this.

Confirming the `--distributed-executor-backend mp` workaround **does** work as described — thanks @jschmied and @dolf3131. On GB10 it puts vLLM on the multiproc path (`multiproc_executor.py:150` in the log), the `PleOffloadWorker` process really does spawn, and the IPC sockets appear in `/tmp` where previously they never did. The original untimed-`Queue.get` hang is gone.

**But on unified memory it then OOMs, and I want to flag that before anyone reads the workaround as a fix on DGX Spark.**

```
(Worker pid=453) RuntimeError: PLE offload worker exited during startup
   (caused by EOFError reading the worker's pipe)
```

The worker did not fail — it was killed by the kernel:

```
oom-kill: constraint=CONSTRAINT_NONE, global_oom, task=python3, pid=2889316
Out of memory: Killed process 2889316 (python3)
   total-vm:272139140kB, anon-rss:42387328kB
oom_reaper: reaped process 2889316
```

42.4 GB resident, i.e. roughly 201/206 of the way through loading the PLE shards, which matches the last `Loading safetensors checkpoint shards(PLE-offload): 98%` line before it died.

**Why:** on GB10 the 128 GB is unified — host and device are the same physical pool — so moving the PLE table "to host RAM" does not create capacity, it just moves the allocation between accounting buckets. Both loads also run concurrently, so the peak is additive:

| | |
|---|---|
| main model (device side) | 86.2 GB (`Model loading took 80.28 GiB`) |
| PLE table (host side) | 51.2 GB |
| **total** | **137.4 GB** |
| usable (`free -g` total) | 121.0 GB |
| **deficit** | **16.4 GB** |

This is checkpoint-specific, not architectural. `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` quantizes the experts to NVFP4 but leaves the PLE shards at FP8 (`model-plefp8-*`, 10 shards, 51.2 GB). At NVFP4 the table would be ~25.6 GB and the total ~111.8 GB, which fits this box with headroom. unsloth's GGUF builds quantize it, so it is clearly possible in principle — I just have not found an NVFP4 checkpoint that does.

Worth noting @jhsmith409 will **not** hit this: 96 GB discrete VRAM plus separate host RAM is two pools, and only ~48 GiB of host is needed. The deficit is specific to unified memory, which is also why the earlier resident figure was misleading — the 80.28 GiB I reported in the original post was measured while the worker had never spawned, so the table was never loaded. That number described the bug, not the feature.

Two small suggestions, both about failure quality rather than the deadlock:

1. **Surface the OOM.** The parent reports `EOFError` → `PLE offload worker exited during startup`, which gives no hint that the kernel killed the child. Checking the child's exit status for `SIGKILL` and saying so would save people a trip to `dmesg`.
2. **A pre-flight capacity check would be cheap.** PLE table size and available memory are both known before loading starts, and on a unified-memory device the correct comparison is against one shared total, not host and device separately. Failing in seconds with "needs 137 GB, have 121 GB" beats OOM-ing 11 minutes into a load.

Happy to test a patch for either on GB10, and to re-run against a build containing 95dc96d1d012 once it lands.

The deficit math is right for RAM-only, but there is a measured configuration on this exact hardware that gets around it: give the box a large swapfile and let the table page. The offload worker keeps the PLE table in pageable host memory by design (only its I/O staging buffers are pinned), so with swap present the cold majority of the table can stay paged out instead of counting against the unified pool.

dolf3131 ran real weights this way on a single GB10 earlier today, on the PR thread: `Inferact/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (170.2 GiB checkpoint whose PLE table is BF16 at 95.37 GB, a strictly worse case than your 51.2 GB), a dedicated 128 GB swapfile, TP=1 with 95dc96d1d012 applied, CUDA graphs on, 524K context, MTP k=3: cold boot to serving in about 13 minutes, decode at 26 to 27.7 tok/s, RAM holding at 104-106 GB used with ~15 GB available. Setup and the corrected throughput numbers: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53899#issuecomment-5436713836

So on a 128 GB Spark the practical ladder looks like: a swapfile today (works now, at whatever paging cost your lookup pattern produces), an NVFP4-quantized PLE table when a checkpoint ships one (your ~111.8 GB estimate fits resident), and your pre-flight capacity check upstream so the failure is legible either way. One refinement to that check given the above actually serves: on unified memory it should probably treat swap-backed capacity as usable-with-degradation rather than fail on the RAM total alone.

**Working single-GB10 configuration, plus a second permission gate this thread has not hit yet.**

Confirming @jahnclawdmonet's swap point with a different checkpoint, and adding a failure that
bites *after* you get past the OOM.

**Config that serves:** `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (125.9 GiB, PLE 47.7 GiB in FP8),
TP=1, `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1`, `--distributed-executor-backend mp`,
`--gpu-memory-utilization 0.90`, 8192 ctx, 64 GiB swapfile.

```
weights resident   76.61 GiB   (81.38 with the MTP draft head)
KV cache           30.99 GiB
free at startup   114.3 / 121.63 GiB
```

So the deficit math in this thread is checkpoint-dependent: with an **FP8** PLE at 47.7 GiB
rather than a BF16 one at 95.37, it fits with room to spare and swap only carries the cold
majority of the table. No OOM across ~15 boots today.

**The second gate: `pidfd_getfd: Operation not permitted`.**

Once past the deadlock and the OOM, the run dies ~10 minutes in — *after* both workers load all
206 shards — with only:

```
RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. Failed core proc(s): {}
```

The real error is upstream in the `PleOffloadWorker` stream:

```
RuntimeError: pidfd_getfd: Operation not permitted
  torch/multiprocessing/reductions.py:179 in rebuild_cuda_tensor
  vllm/v1/ple_offload/worker.py:482 in accept_registrations
```

Cause is **`kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1`**, the default on Ubuntu and DGX OS. It restricts
`PTRACE_MODE_ATTACH` — which `pidfd_getfd` requires — to **descendants only**, and
`PleOffloadWorker` and the GPU worker are *siblings*, both children of the engine. So the
CUDA-IPC tensor handoff in `accept_registrations` is refused.

| deployment | fix |
|---|---|
| Docker | `--cap-add=SYS_PTRACE` |
| bare metal / systemd | `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_SYS_PTRACE` |
| bare metal / shell | inherits the login's caps; usually already works |

For systemd, `cap_sys_ptrace` in `CapabilityBoundingSet` is **not** sufficient — a `User=` service
holds no effective capabilities without `AmbientCapabilities`. `sysctl kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0`
also works but weakens ptrace machine-wide.

I first reported this as a Docker seccomp restriction and that was wrong; I found out by building
the same stack bare metal, where it failed identically. `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` bypasses yama, which is
why the Docker flag worked for the wrong reason. It does **not** affect mmap-based PLE approaches
(single process, no IPC handoff), which is likely why it has stayed invisible.

Suggestion: since the engine reports `Failed core proc(s): {}` and hides the cause ten minutes
into a load, a preflight check on `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD` — read `/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope`
and warn if it is non-zero and `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` is absent — would save a lot of people that
round-trip. Happy to send a PR if that seems reasonable.

**Working numbers on this box, TP=1**, in case they help anyone size a run — single-stream decode
17.1 tok/s unspeculated, **28.5 with in-checkpoint MTP k=2** (mean accepted length 2.36), and
aggregate 266.8 tok/s at 48 concurrent streams with TTFT 1.6 s.

**Third reproduction, on discrete VRAM, with every previously-proposed cause ruled out - plus a
correction to two claims in this thread.**

driver 610.57.04, CUDA 13.3, x86_64, 246 GB host RAM. Image `vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next-x86_64-cu129`
(`sha256:f16a96245c0a`, vLLM `0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198`). TP=1, `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1`.

I backported 95dc96d1d012 into the shipped image (mounted `uniproc_executor.py`) and confirmed it

**This second stall was fixed upstream on 2026-08-29, about three hours before the most recent
comment here.** #53899 picked up `4e8b849b8d97` — *"[BugFix] fix PLE offload for async MRV2
scheduling"* — and it addresses exactly the `_copy_cuda_inputs` frame that @estrella159 and
@sebastiancretu both captured. Posting because three people appear to be debugging something that
already has a fix.

**What was wrong.** In the shipped `0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198` tree, `PleOffloadConnector` allocates
**one** `_input_ready_event` and **one** `_d2h_done_event` for the whole connector
(`connector.py:120-122`), on the stated assumption that only one request is ever outstanding:

```python
# PLE rejects DBO, and each forward consumes its output before the
# next launch, so one pending request is sufficient.
self._request_queue = queue.Queue(maxsize=1)
```

That assumption does not hold under async scheduling, where `max_concurrent_batches == 2` and the
host runs a batch ahead. The request thread pops a request immediately, so the queue is empty while
request #1 is still being staged, and `_launch(#2)` re-records the *same* `_input_ready_event` on
the model stream — now enqueued behind forward #1's PLE semaphore wait, which cannot clear until
request #1 has been sent. The offload thread is meanwhile inside
`self._d2h_stream.wait_event(self._input_ready_event)` waiting on that newer record. The main
thread's device-wide `torch.accelerator.synchronize()` at the end of `warmup_kernels` waits on the
D2H stream too, so nothing retires.

That accounts for the observations the PCIe explanation does not:

- **Unified memory reproduces it** (@sebastiancretu, GX10). The copies are cheap; it is the *wait*
  that hangs, so no real transfer is required.
- **`--enforce-eager` serves** (@estrella159). Eager keeps the host from running far enough ahead to
  re-record the event before the offload thread has sent request #1 — it narrows the window, it does
  not remove the race.
- **It is intermittent across identical boots on an air-gapped box** (@sebastiancretu, third
  restart, no changes). A shared-event race behaves this way; a deterministic code path does not.
- **Worker idle, 0% on every engine, no Xid.** Consistent with a stream-ordering cycle.

**What the fix does.** `4e8b849b8d97` introduces `_PendingPleOffloadRequest`, binding each request
to its own event drawn from a pool sized `max_concurrent_batches`; sizes `_request_queue` the same
way; drops `_d2h_stream` and the cross-stream `wait_event` entirely, issuing the staging copies on
the **model** stream (`_enqueue_cuda_inputs`); and leaves the offload thread doing only
`event.synchronize()`.

**Possible workaround before you can rebuild:** `--no-async-scheduling` (it is a
`BooleanOptionalAction`, so `--async-scheduling=False` is an argparse error). With
`pipeline_parallel_size=1` that puts `max_concurrent_batches` at 1, so only one request is ever in
flight and the shared event cannot be re-recorded mid-staging.

I want to be clear about the status of that suggestion: it is **derived from the code, not verified
against the bug**, because I cannot reproduce the hang here (see below). If it holds it should cost
far less than `--enforce-eager`. Someone who *can* reproduce it would settle it in one start.

Note this is on by default: `async_scheduling` resolves to `None` → `True` for a decode model on an
executor that supports it, and both `mp` and `uniproc` report `supports_async_scheduling() == True`,
so every configuration in this thread has two batches in flight unless it was turned off explicitly.

**A negative control, and what the flag costs.** On a single GB10 (unified, TP=1,
`--distributed-executor-backend mp`, `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1`, `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`
with an FP8 head, 8192 ctx, 64 GiB swap, `cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE` with capture sizes
`[1,2,4,8]`) I have **not been able to reproduce this hang at all** — across many restarts, with
MTP k=2 and with speculation off, and with async scheduling left at its default (on). So I cannot
confirm that `--no-async-scheduling` fixes it; I can only say the race is real in the code and that
upstream has replaced the shared events.

What I can report is that the flag is **cheap**, at least here (median of n=6 runs; our noise floor
is 6.9%):

| | async scheduling on | `--no-async-scheduling` |
|---|---|---|
| c=1 decode tok/s | 36.45 ± 1.04 | 36.6 / 37.0 / 34.8 |
| c=16 aggregate tok/s | 99.1 / 101.5 / 100.1 | 101.6 / 100.8 |

No measurable cost either way. One caveat worth stating: this box is memory-bandwidth-bound at
c=16 (~100 tok/s aggregate is a ceiling here, not a scheduling artifact — I checked by raising
`--max-num-seqs` from 16 to 64, which changed nothing), so async scheduling's CPU/GPU overlap has
little to hide. On a less bandwidth-bound setup the flag may well cost something.

We hit this reliably on a GB10 (sm_121, aarch64) single-GPU TP=1 serve of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, and traced it to a startup rendezvous race in the PLE CPU-offload path: when the registration handoff is lost, the GPU worker's first warmup forward enqueues an untimed `cuStreamWaitValue32` that the offload process never signals, while the offload worker's registration `recv` and `wait_for_engine_startup` both wait unbounded — so the boot hangs forever after "Registrations complete" / "Worker ready". TP2/TP4 sibling-rank timing masks the race, which is why it only shows up on single GPU, flaky by rendezvous luck. A hung boot never reaches EngineCore's "init engine" log line, which is a quick way to tell this hang from a slow cold boot.

Fix here (PR into the #53899 source branch, since the offload code isn't on main yet): https://github.com/peakcrosser7/vllm/pull/10
Branch: https://github.com/davidtai/vllm/tree/fix/ple-cpu-offload-tp1-startup-deadlock

Three parts: (1) a startup barrier — the GPU worker binds a private ACK endpoint before registering and blocks until the offload worker acknowledges, ordering offload-ready before the first warmup forward; (2) bounded, named startup timeouts on the registration recv, the ACK wait, and `wait_for_engine_startup`, so a lost rendezvous fails loudly instead of hanging; (3) startup-phase-only scoping — blocking recv is restored before `busy_loop`, so the steady-state decode path is unchanged (verified bit-identical outputs and unchanged decode rate on the same machine). The same patch applies onto the #54070 disk-offload stack with only context drift.

### The finding: `pidfd_getfd` is not Docker-specific

@jschmied hit `pidfd_getfd: Operation not permitted` and reasonably read it as a
rootless-Docker capability problem. **It is not.** I hit it on bare metal, no container
anywhere, running as an ordinary user — and it fails *deterministically*, not by luck:

```
accept_registrations -> pickle.loads -> rebuild_cuda_tensor -> _new_shared_cuda
RuntimeError: pidfd_getfd: Operation not permitted
```

The mechanism is the process direction. The GPU worker hands the offload process a CUDA
IPC tensor handle; rebuilding it makes **`PleOffloadWorker` (the child) ptrace-attach to
`VLLM::Worker` (its parent)**. Yama `ptrace_scope=1` permits attaching to *descendants*
only, and a parent is never a descendant of its child — so scope 1 fails 100% of the time
here, on any distro that defaults to 1 (Arch, Debian, Ubuntu). Docker was incidental.

Fix is one sysctl:

```bash
echo 'kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-ptrace.conf
sudo sysctl --system
```

A narrower alternative, if someone wants to keep scope 1 machine-wide, is
`prctl(PR_SET_PTRACER, PR_SET_PTRACER_ANY)` in the GPU worker before it spawns the
offload process — that scopes the exemption to the one process instead of the host.
That might be worth doing in-tree, since the current failure mode is genuinely
misleading: weights load fine, `PleOffload: registered` prints *success*, and then the
API server simply never binds `:8000`. It looks like the hangs in this thread but is a
completely different cause.

Directly observed, with a real before/after — `ptrace_scope=1` → EPERM every time;
`ptrace_scope=0` → boots clean, same binary, same flags.

### Checkpoint choice matters more than it looks

Most reports here use `RadixArk/...-NVFP4` (FP8 PLE, 47.7 GiB), which needs an
out-of-tree load patch because of #54765. I used **`Inferact/...-NVFP4`, whose PLE table
is BF16** — it carries no `weight_scale` tensor, so #54765 cannot fire and no load patch
is needed. Cost is 95.37 GiB of host RAM instead of 47.7, which is free on a discrete
box. If you have host RAM to spare, this removes a patch from the stack.
